notes.b: A cereal grain is the seed of a grass, and the wheat grain is the standard example. It has three parts, and its nutrients are spread unevenly across them, so what you eat depends on which parts are kept.
points: Bran: the outer covering, made of several layers, about 13% of the wheat grain. It is made mainly of cellulose, an insoluble fibre, and it is removed when white flour is milled.

Endosperm: the inner and largest part of the grain. It stores starch, and it also contains most of the grain's protein, which forms gluten when wheat flour is mixed with water. White flour is made from it, and it is the food store for the young plant.
Germ: the small embryo at the base of the grain, about 2% of the grain, which would grow into a new plant. It is rich in vitamin E, unsaturated fat, protein and B group vitamins.
Diagram: longitudinal section (cut lengthways) of the wheat grain, showing bran around the outside, a large endosperm, and the germ at the base. Label all three parts and the crease along one side.
notes.tip: You may be asked to identify grain parts from a description or fill gaps: the endosperm is the largest part and is starch, the bran is cellulose, and the germ is small and sits at the base.

notes.b: Each part of the grain supplies different nutrients, so you need to name the nutrient and say what it does in the body.
points: Bran: its cellulose is dietary fibre (roughage), which adds bulk to faeces, absorbs water and stimulates peristalsis (the muscle waves that push food along the gut). This prevents constipation and aids digestion.
Bran also supplies B group vitamins and minerals such as iron, magnesium and phosphorus.

Endosperm: starch is the main carbohydrate in cereals and supplies energy for heat and activity. The protein it contains is of low biological value, meaning it is low in one or more essential amino acids.
Germ: it supplies most of the grain's unsaturated fat, and vitamin E, which acts as an antioxidant (it protects body cells from damage).
Germ: it also supplies protein and B group vitamins such as thiamine (vitamin B1), which are concentrated in the germ.
Refining removes most of the bran and germ, so white flour and refined cereals lose most of their fibre, B group vitamins, vitamin E and minerals unless these are added back.
notes.tip: Marks go for a relevant nutrient and its function: bran gives fibre for peristalsis, B vitamins and iron; endosperm gives starch for energy and protein; germ gives unsaturated fat, vitamin E and B vitamins. Do not give B vitamins or vitamin E as endosperm nutrients, because they are concentrated in the bran and germ.

notes.b: The nutritive value of a food is the nutrients it supplies. Cereals are mainly a starchy food, with smaller amounts of several other nutrients.
points: Protein: provides protein for growth and repair of body cells, but cereal protein is of low biological value because it is low in the essential amino acid lysine (an amino acid the body cannot make).
Eating cereals with pulses, milk or eggs improves the protein's value, because the foods make up for each other's missing amino acids (complementary proteins).
Carbohydrate: starch provides energy for heat and activity, and wholegrain cereals also provide fibre.
Fibre: wholegrain cereals provide insoluble fibre from the bran, and oats and barley provide soluble fibre.
Fat: cereals are low in total fat, and the fat they contain is mainly unsaturated and concentrated in the germ.
Vitamins: B group vitamins (thiamine, niacin and riboflavin) and vitamin E, which is found in the germ.
Minerals: calcium, iron and phosphorus, much of the iron and phosphorus being found in the bran and germ.
Water: cereals are dry foods with a low water content, so they keep well when stored correctly.
notes.tip: Cereal protein is low biological value, not high. An account of nutritive value usually needs several separate points, so give the nutrient and, where you can, its role or location in the grain.

notes.b: The dietetic value of a food is how useful it is in the diet, for health and for everyday eating. Cereals score well for cost, fibre and convenience, with a few limits.
points: Energy: starchy cereals are an inexpensive source of energy and form the staple food (the food a diet is built around) in many countries.
Constipation: the fibre in wholegrain cereals increases stool bulk and stimulates peristalsis, so it helps prevent constipation and bowel disorders.
Blood cholesterol and blood sugar: soluble fibre from oats and barley can help lower blood cholesterol and slows the absorption of glucose after a meal.
Satiety (feeling full): fibre-rich foods give a feeling of fullness, which supports weight control.
Fat: the fat in cereals is unsaturated, so it does not contribute to cholesterol build-up.
Versatility: cereals can be used in sweet and savoury dishes, and they are quick and easy to prepare and inexpensive.
Limit, coeliac disease: gluten, found in wheat, barley and rye, and in oats unless they are labelled gluten-free, cannot be tolerated by people with coeliac disease.
Limit, phytic acid: phytic acid in the bran binds iron and calcium (so the body cannot absorb them) and reduces their absorption.
notes.tip: Typical answers give two nutritive and two dietetic points plus one other, so include dietetic points such as energy, fibre, versatility, cost, unsaturated fat, and gluten and phytic acid as limits.

notes.h: Wholegrain cereals (evaluating their contribution to a healthy diet)
notes.b: A wholegrain cereal keeps the whole grain rather than just the starchy centre. This is why wholegrain products are promoted as part of a healthy diet.
points: A wholegrain cereal product contains all three parts of the grain: bran, endosperm and germ. Examples are wholemeal flour and bread, brown rice, porridge oats, wholegrain breakfast cereals and wholewheat pasta.

Wholegrain products provide more fibre, B group vitamins, vitamin E and minerals than refined products made from the same cereal. They also release energy more slowly and are filling, so their fibre raises fibre intake.
In the Food Pyramid, wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice form the second shelf, so wholegrain choices fit into the balance of the whole diet.
Phytic acid in the bran binds iron, calcium and zinc and reduces their absorption; very high fibre intakes can have the same effect.
Beans on wholemeal toast is an example of combining cereal protein with pulses, which raises the biological value of the protein.
A wholegrain label does not cancel excess sugar, fat or salt added to some products, so the nutrition panel must still be checked.
A high-fibre day for a school child could use wholegrain breakfast cereal, brown bread, and brown rice or wholewheat pasta.
notes.tip: At Higher Level you may be asked to evaluate wholegrain cereals: say all three parts are kept, give more fibre and nutrients than refined, name the benefits and the drawbacks, and balance them in the whole diet. Wholegrain is not the same as brown or multigrain: a brown loaf made from refined flour is not wholegrain.

notes.b: Cereals are healthy for most people, but some people avoid or limit them for medical or dietary reasons.
points: Coeliac disease or gluten intolerance: gluten damages the lining of the small intestine, so gluten-containing cereals must be avoided.
Weight gain: large portions of starchy foods, especially with added fat or sugar, supply more energy than the body uses, so low-carbohydrate or weight-loss diets limit them.
Blood sugar: refined cereals are digested quickly and raise blood glucose quickly, so people managing blood sugar, or following low glycaemic index diets, often choose wholegrain cereals.
Bloating: some people limit cereals because they cause bloating.
Hidden salt and sugar: many breakfast cereals, breads and sauces contain added salt or sugar.
Main sources of cereals in the Irish diet are bread, pasta, rice, breakfast cereals, porridge, biscuits and cakes.
notes.tip: Exams ask for reasons some people limit cereals, and for the main sources of cereals in the Irish diet, so learn both lists.

B group vitamins: help the body release energy from carbohydrate and keep the nervous system and skin healthy. Full marks for any two relevant nutrients from the bran (fibre, B group vitamins, iron, magnesium, phosphorus) with a correct function for each.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the nutritive and dietetic value of wholegrain cereals contributes to a healthy diet, and identify one limitation of relying on cereals as a source of nutrients.
questions.model: Structure: wholegrain cereals keep the bran, endosperm and germ, so they contribute more nutrients than refined cereals. Nutritive value: starch from the endosperm supplies energy; the protein is of low biological value and is low in lysine, so pulses improve its quality; fibre from the bran and the germ's unsaturated fat, vitamin E and B group vitamins supply nutrients; iron, calcium and phosphorus are provided. Dietetic value: fibre prevents constipation and adds bulk; soluble fibre from oats and barley helps lower blood cholesterol and slows glucose absorption; fibre promotes fullness for weight control; cereals are inexpensive, versatile and quick to prepare. Limitation: gluten makes wheat, barley and rye unsuitable for people with coeliac disease; phytic acid reduces mineral absorption; a wholegrain label does not cancel high sugar, fat or salt, so the whole diet must be balanced.
